Borrowed from Late Latin abstractiō.

parole.significato: acolyte, altar boy (generally, an assistant who performs liturgical duties such as carrying the wine, water and lights…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, helper”).
From Late Latin anacolūthon
From Late Latin anamnēsis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάμνησις (anámnēsis, “calling to mind, reminiscence”), from ἀνα- (ana-) + μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, remember”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin annihilō
Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + πόδες (pódes), nominative plural of πούς (poús, “foot”).

From Late Latin poplexia, apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”); ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

From Late Latin archīvum (“public records office”).
From Late Latin astralis, from Latin astrum (“star”) + -ālis, the first element from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).

Borrowed from Late Latin breve.
From Middle High German burse, from Old High German bursa, from Late Latin bursa.
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
From Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).

Middle High German dissonantz, from Late Latin dissonantia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), from Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis.
Borrowed from Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “play, drama”, noun), from δρᾰ́ω (drắō, “do, act”, verb) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominalizing suffix). First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Late Latin duālitās.

parole.significato: editor (person at a newspaper, publisher or similar institution who edits stories)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēditor.
Via a Romance language, compare French endive, Italian indivia, from Late Latin intibus.
Borrowed from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós).
From Middle High German erz-, erze-, from Old High German erzi-, from Late Latin archi-, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-).

parole.significato: screed, floor made of cement or plaster (as an intermediate layer below the flooring, or for immediate use)
parole.testo: From Middle High German esterich, estrich, from Old High German estrih, asterih, from Late Latin astracum, astricum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “potsherd”).

parole.significato: ethics (study of principles governing right and wrong conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ex tunc.
From Late Latin exorbitāns.
Borrowed from Late Latin extēnsīvus (“extending”), influenced by French extensif and its antonym intensif.

parole.significato: firmament (the sky, especially when conceived as a dome)
parole.testo: From Middle High German firmament, from Late Latin firmāmentum.

parole.significato: germander (any plant of the genus Teucrium)
parole.testo: From Middle High German gamandrē, from Late Latin gamandrea, chamandrea, from Latin chamaedrys, from Ancient Greek χαμαίδρῡς (khamaídrūs, literally “ground-oak”).
From Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).

From Middle High German glocke, glogge, from Old High German klocca, from Late Latin clocca, probably of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”) (compare Welsh cloch, Irish clog), from Proto-Indo-European *klēg-, *klōg- (onomatopoeia). Cognate with Vilamovian głok and English clock.

parole.significato: column, squib (short, witty and often satirical piece of newspaper writing regarding current events)
parole.testo: From Middle High German glōse, from Late Latin glōssa. The modern spelling with -ss- is from renewed influence by the Latin spelling in the 17th century, despite maintaining the pronunciation with /oː/ in technical usage.

parole.significato: the character of the Ancient Greek language, customs, or culture; Hellenism
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Graecitās.
From Middle High German gupf, gupfe (“highest point”), possibly from Late Latin cuppa (“cup”). Related to Gipfel, Kuppe and Kuppel.

From Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὑπνῶ (hupnô, “I put to sleep”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

parole.significato: inspiration (exercising an elevating or stimulating influence upon the intellect or emotions)
parole.testo: Learned 16th century borrowing from Late Latin īnspīrātiō, from Latin īnspīrātus, perfect participle of īnspīrō (“to breathe in, to inhale”), + -tiō.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūbilaeum, from iūbilaeus.
From Late Latin iūdaismus, from Koine Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós).

parole.significato: pulpit; raised, enclosed platform in a church from which a preacher preaches
parole.testo: From Middle High German kanzel, Old High German cancella (“the place set apart for the priests”); derived from Late Latin cancellus (“grating”). Cognate with English chancel.
From Middle High German kanzelie, itself borrowed from Late Latin cancellarius (“secretary, porter”).
From Middle High German kappelle, kapelle, from Old High German kappella, kapella, from Late Latin and Vulgar Latin cappella (“chapel”).
From Late Latin carentia (“being without”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin carminātus.

parole.significato: catalogue (systematic list of names, books, pictures, etc.; complete list of items; university calendar)
parole.testo: From Late Latin catalogus, from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length”), from κατά (katá, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, to pick up, to choose for oneself, to pick out, to count”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēchismus.
From Late Latin catēgoria (compare Yiddish קאַטעגאָריע (kategorye)), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
Borrowed from Late Latin causālis.

From Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen, via French criminel.
From Late Latin crypticus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch, from Ancient Greek κρυπτικός (kruptikós). Cognate to English cryptic.

From Middle High German kupfe, from Old High German kupfa (“cap, bonnet”), probably from Late Latin cuppa (“cup”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German koppe. Cognate with Dutch kop (“cup; head”), English cup. Related also with Kopf (“head”).

From Middle High German legende (“story of a saint”), from Late Latin legenda.

From Middle High German litanīe, from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).
Borrowed from Late Latin magnātus, derived from magnus (“great”). The historic senses are influenced by Polish magnat, Hungarian mágnás, both from the same Latin word.
From Middle High German matte, from Old High German matta, from Late Latin matta, from a Semitic language.
From Middle High German mesnære, from Old High German mesināri, from Late Latin mānsiōnārius, from mānsiō (“dwelling, abode”).
From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From Middle High German mettī, from Old High German mattina, a borrowing of Late Latin mattina from Classical Latin (laudēs) mātūtīnae (“morning (praise)”).
Borrowed from Late Latin moloch, from Hebrew מולך.
From Late Latin monumentālis, via French monumental.

parole.significato: moratorium (suspension or delaying of an activity or process)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin morātōrium, nominalized neuter singular of morātōrius.

parole.significato: consecrated wafer, host (small thin round piece of unleavened bread)
parole.testo: From Middle High German oblāte f, oblāt f, from Old High German oblāta, from Late Latin oblāta (“offered”), past participle of offerō.
From Middle High German oblāt m, from Late Latin oblātus (“person dedicated to religious life”), a nominal use of the past participle of offerō (“to offer”).
From Late Latin officialis.
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).

From Middle High German phingesten, from Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ). The Old High German form fimfchusti is a partial calque of the Ancient Greek term, with πεντη- (pentē-) replaced by fimf (“five”). Cognate with Hunsrik Pingste and Dutch Pinksteren.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin Pharaō.

parole.significato: stone pine (Pinus pinea, a chiefly Mediterranean tree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin pīnea (“pine”), from Latin pīnus (“pine tree”).
Borrowed from Late Latin pistācia.

Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós, “abundance; excess”).

parole.significato: internship (job taken by a student), apprenticeship

From Late Latin practicus, influenced by French pratique.

From Late Latin praedicātum.
From Late Latin praevalentia, from Latin praevaleō.
From Middle High German punct, Late Latin pūnctus. Doublet of bunt.

parole.significato: limited to specific, selected points or instances (as opposed to being common, compehensive or otherwise large-scale)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin pūnctuālis, possibly through French ponctuel with the vocalism realigned with Punkt.

From Late Latin rubro gilum (“red brook”), of Celtic origin; for the second element see the river Celbis.

parole.testo: From Middle High German secte, from Late Latin secta (“a sect in philosophy or religion, a school, faction”), possibly from Latin sequī (“to follow”).

parole.significato: sequestrum (a fragment of bone or other dead tissue)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin sequestrare (“to separate”), from Latin sequester (“mediating”), from Latin sequi (“to follow”). Compare sequestrieren.

parole.significato: a form of sexual intercourse considered perverse and unnatural; sodomy
parole.testo: From Late Latin sodomia, from the Biblical town Sodom (Genesis 18f.), from Ancient Greek Σόδομα (Sódoma), from Hebrew סדם (səḏōm).

Borrowed from Late Latin synodālis, from synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos, “assembly, meeting”). Cognate with English synodal, Dutch synodaal, French synodal.

parole.significato: table (grid of data in rows and columns)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tabella (“small table”), 16th c.

parole.significato: to press (to extract juice from fruits, especially grapes)
parole.testo: From late Middle High German torkeln, from Late Latin torculo (“to press”), a derivation of Latin torculum (“wine press”).
Borrowed from Late Latin trānsgressiō.
Borrowed from Late Latin trias.
Borrowed from Late Latin valentia (“vigour”), shortened from ealier Quantivalenz.

parole.significato: verbosity (the excess use of words; long-windedness)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin verbōsitās. Compare verbosit.

From Middle High German voget, from Old High German fogat, borrowed from Late Latin vocātus, from Classical Latin advocātus. Doublet of Advokat.

parole.significato: onion (typically Allium cepa, the plant or its bulb)
parole.testo: From Middle High German zwibel, zwibolle, from Old High German zwibollo, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.
From Late Latin aequidistāns, possibly via Middle French équidistant.
Borrowed from Late Latin aera.
